topic: Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif, and Zaid
description: Indian agriculture is highly dependent on the monsoon and changing weather patterns. Based on variations in climate and temperature, India broadly has three distinct cropping seasons: Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid.

sections.title: Introduction to Indian Agricultural Seasons
sections.description: The geographical diversity and climatic conditions of India dictate the agricultural cycle and cropping patterns across different regions.

key_concepts.explanation: The practice of growing different types of crops sequentially on the same piece of land to maintain soil fertility and reduce pest buildup.
Based on parameters like temperature, rainfall, and soil types, the erstwhile Planning Commission of India divided the country into 15 distinct agro-climatic zones.

sections.title: Kharif Season
sections.description: The agricultural season that begins with the onset of the monsoon, requiring high temperatures, high humidity, and plenty of water.

key_concepts.explanation: These crops are sown at the beginning of the monsoon season (June-July) and harvested at the end of the monsoon season (September-October).

key_associations.extra_info: West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, and Punjab are among the top producing states. It requires high rainfall and standing water.
Predominantly grown in the black soil (Regur) regions of Gujarat and Maharashtra.
Madhya Pradesh is the leading producer, often referred to as the 'Soya State' of India.

important_facts.fact: In states like Assam, West Bengal, and Odisha, three crops of paddy are grown in a single year, locally known as Aus, Aman, and Boro.

sections.title: Rabi Season
sections.description: The agricultural season consisting of winter crops that require cool temperatures for growth and a warm climate for seed maturation.

key_concepts.explanation: These crops are sown in winter (October-November) and harvested in summer (April-May). They require cold weather for germination and warm weather for ripening.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: North and North-Western India (Punjab, Haryana, Western UP)
geographical_data.key_characteristics: The winter rainfall caused by 'Western Disturbances' originating in the Mediterranean Sea is highly beneficial for the success of these crops.

key_associations.extra_info: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Punjab are the top producers.
Extensively cultivated in the semi-arid regions of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.

important_facts.fact: The success of the Green Revolution in the late 1960s was most prominent in boosting the production of Rabi crops, particularly wheat, in North-Western India.

sections.title: Zaid Season
sections.description: A short cropping season during the summer months lying between the Rabi and Kharif seasons.

key_concepts.explanation: Short-term crops grown from March to June. They require warm, dry weather for major growth periods and longer day length for flowering.

key_associations.extra_info: These are predominantly grown on river banks and in sandy soils across the country.

key_associations.item: Cucumber, Bitter Gourd, and Fodder Crops
key_associations.extra_info: Cultivated across India wherever proper irrigation facilities are available during the dry summer months.

sections.title: Economic Classification of Crops
sections.description: Besides seasons, crops are also classified based on their ultimate use and economic value.

key_concepts.explanation: Crops grown primarily for sale in the market to earn profit, rather than for the farmer's own consumption.
A type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on a large estate. It is capital-intensive and relies heavily on migrant labour.

key_associations.extra_info: Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra are the top producers. It is a long-duration crop that takes almost a year to mature.
Tea is heavily cultivated in Assam and West Bengal (Darjeeling), while Coffee is predominantly grown in Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.
Also known as the 'Golden Fibre'. West Bengal is the undisputed leading producer in India.
